item.title: Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on the Status of the U.S.-EU Détente Following Record-Breaking Loan from the European Investment Bank to Airbus
item.description:
Ambassador Greer Issues Statement on the Status of the U.S.-EU Détente Following Record-Breaking Loan from the European Investment Bank to Airbus pbrouillette Mon, 10/26/2026 - 18:59

WASHINGTON — Today, Ambassador Jamieson Greer issued a statement regarding the status of the U.S.-EU deal to pause duties on certain EU imports, following a record-breaking loan from the European Investment Bank to Airbus.

“I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past,” said Ambassador Greer. “For decades, France, Germany, and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over U.S. aerospace workers and businesses. After winning at the WTO and imposing significant U.S. duties on EU imports in response, USTR struck a deal with the EU to pause those duties in exchange for a mutual commitment to provide financing to large civil aircraft (LCA) producers on market terms. Yet, this summer, almost immediately after the EU extended this pause, the European Investment Bank awarded Airbus its largest loan ever to benefit Airbus projects in France, Germany, and Spain. Despite ongoing requests, USTR still has no details about this loan. This situation injects substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector. It is important this situation is resolved as soon as possible to ensure market-driven production in the aerospace sector and to avoid violation of the terms of our hard-won LCA deal.”

item.title: United States Announces Successful Resolution of Rapid Response Labor Mechanism Matter at Amphenol Optimize
item.description:
United States Announces Successful Resolution of Rapid Response Labor Mechanism Matter at Amphenol Optimize pbrouillette Fri, 10/23/2026 - 16:06

WASHINGTON — The United States today announced the successful resolution of the USMCA Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) matter at the Amphenol Optimize México, S.A. de C.V. (Amphenol) facility located in Nogales, Sonora, Mexico, which manufactures automotive and aerospace connectors, cables, and components. The United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation to address labor rights violations occurring at the facility, including employer interference in union activity and retaliatory dismissals of workers. That plan has now been implemented, and the Denial of Rights concerns raised in the U.S. request for review have been remediated. As a result, the United States Trade Representative has directed the Secretary of the Treasury to resume liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the facility.

Actions taken by the facility to address the matter include: 

  • Reinstating nine workers with full backpay and benefits; 
  • Implementing a neutrality statement and guidelines related to the freedom of association and collective bargaining; and
  • Installing and publicizing a complaint mechanism through which workers can report violations of their rights and breaches of company policies.

Actions taken by the Government of Mexico to address the matter include: 

  • Delivering in-person trainings for all company personnel on the freedom of association and collective bargaining; 
  • Monitoring the facility and engaging with workers and the company throughout its review period; and
  • Maintaining a direct email address, reporting platform, and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, and timely investigating any allegations.

Background

The United States Trade Representative and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On April 11, 2025, the ILC received an RRM petition from the Sindicato Industrial Operaciones y Manufacturas, a Mexican labor union. The petition alleged that Amphenol had violated workers’ right to freedom of association and collective bargaining by coercing workers to vote for the company-favored outcome during a union vote, discouraging workers from joining an independent union, and taking reprisals against workers due to their union preferences, including through dismissals. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms.  
 
As a result, on May 9, 2025, the United States Trade Representative submitted a request to Mexico to review the matter. Mexico accepted the request, conducted an investigation, and worked with Amphenol to provide remediation to dismissed workers and implement facility-wide measures aimed at safeguarding freedom of association and collective bargaining rights. The United States has reviewed the matter and concluded the situation to have been remediated.  

As a result of the above actions taken by the facility and Mexico to resolve the action, the United States agrees that there is no ongoing denial of rights. Ambassador Greer’s letter directing the Secretary of the Treasury to resume liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the facility is available here.

Read the full course of remediation here.

Read an unofficial courtesy Spanish translation of the full course of remediation here.

Information about previous requests can be found here.

item.title: United States and Mexico Announce Course of Remediation at Minera Peñasquito
item.description:
United States and Mexico Announce Course of Remediation at Minera Peñasquito pbrouillette Fri, 10/23/2026 - 09:06

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative and the Government of Mexico (Mexico) today announced a course of remediation at Minera Peñasquito, S.A. de C.V. (Newmont Peñasquito), located in the state of Zacatecas, Mexico. The remediation plan will help ensure workers at the facility can freely exercise their right to freedom of association and collective bargaining.  

Actions already taken by the company to address the matter include:  

  • Posting and dissemination of a neutrality statement and company guidelines on freedom of association and collective bargaining; and
  • Installation of a complaint mechanism for workers to report violations of their rights anonymously and confidentially.

Under the course of remediation, Mexico will ensure that Newmont Peñasquito will, among other things:

  • Reinstate and provide full backpay and benefits to two workers; 
  • Distribute hard copies of the neutrality statement and company guidelines related to freedom of association and collective bargaining to all company personnel;
  • Implement the neutrality statement and company guidelines on freedom of association and collective bargaining, including a zero-tolerance policy for violations; 
  • Publicly acknowledge, through meetings with the workers and postings at the facility, the company’s unlawful and interfering practices;
  • Conduct in-person training for all company personnel during work hours regarding rights related to freedom of association and collective bargaining; and
  • Maintain its complaint mechanism for workers to report violations of their rights anonymously and confidentially.

Under the course of remediation, Mexico will:

  • Review and facilitate the reinstatement and severance processes to ensure two workers receive reinstatement offers and full backpay and benefits, or full severance payments, as applicable; and
  • Maintain a direct email address and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of workers’ freedom of association and collective bargaining rights.

The United States and Mexico agreed to establish a deadline of October 28, 2026 to complete the course of remediation.

Background

The United States Trade Representative and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On May 13, 2026, the ILC received an RRM petition from the Sindicato Nacional de Trabajadores Mineros, Metalúrgicos, Siderúrgicos y Similares de la República Mexicana (Los Mineros), a Mexican labor union. The petition alleged that Newmont Peñasquito had violated workers’ rights by retaliating against workers for engaging in union activity, including through unlawful dismissals. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.

The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms. As a result, the United States Trade Representative submitted a request that Mexico review whether workers at Newmont Peñasquito were being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. Mexico agreed to conduct a review. Following Mexico’s investigation, the United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation.

Read the full course of remediation here.

item.title: United States Announces Successful Resolution of Rapid Response Labor Mechanism Matter at Alimentos Grole Facility
item.description:
United States Announces Successful Resolution of Rapid Response Labor Mechanism Matter at Alimentos Grole Facility pbrouillette Mon, 10/19/2026 - 14:41

WASHINGTON – The United States today announced the successful resolution of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) facility-specific Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) matter regarding the Alimentos Grole, S.A. de C.V. (Alimentos Grole or the company) facility in Ciudad Obregón, Sonora, Mexico, where workers alleged they were previously denied their freedom of association and collective bargaining rights. The United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation to address labor rights violations occurring at the facility, including the formation of a company-aligned internal labor committee and retaliatory dismissals of workers. That plan has now been implemented, and the denial of rights concerns raised in our request for review have been remediated. As a result, the United States Trade Representative has directed the Secretary of the Treasury to resume liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the facility.

Actions taken by the facility to address the matter include:

  • Reinstating nine unlawfully dismissed workers with full backpay and benefits and paying full severance to two workers, based on their respective preferences;
  • Disbanding the company-aligned internal labor committee and ceasing and desisting from utilizing it or encouraging or supporting the formation of any such committee in the future;
  • Developing a facility access protocol that allows the Mexican labor union Sindicato de Trabajadores de la Industria Alimentaria, Mantenimiento Industrial, Similares y Conexos del Estado de Sonora (SITIES) to exercise its rights and perform its duties;
  • Restructuring human resources and labor relations management, and taking appropriate disciplinary action against staff who violated workers’ freedom of association and collective bargaining rights;
  • Implementing and training all company personnel on its neutrality statement intended to ensure there is an environment in which freedom of association and collective bargaining rights are realized without employer interference, and guidelines related to freedom of association and collective bargaining, including a zero-tolerance policy for violations, and committing to retraining as needed;
  • Informing workers about the denial of rights at the facility by conducting meetings and posting notices at the facility to acknowledge Alimentos Grole’s unlawful and interfering practices and affirm the company’s intention to respect workers’ rights in the future;
  • Installing and publicizing a complaint mechanism through which workers can report violations of their rights and breaches of company policies anonymously and confidentially; and
  • Maintaining on the company website and in any internal communications platform the neutrality statement and guidelines, collective bargaining agreement, training materials, and information about complaint mechanisms maintained by the company and the Government of Mexico (Mexico), such that the information is easily accessible to workers.

Actions taken by Mexico to address the matter include:

  • Monitoring the facility to ensure compliance with the obligations in the course of remediation and compliance with Mexican laws related to freedom of association and collective bargaining;
  • Conducting in-person trainings that are structured to ensure all workers understand their right to freedom of association and collective bargaining and how to exercise it, including by informing workers of the denial of rights at the facility and educating workers on the conciliation process available to any dismissed worker;
  • Conducting a separate workers’ rights training for supervisors, human resources and labor relations personnel, and other high-level and “trusted” officials; and
  • Maintaining a direct email address, reporting platform, and telephone line for workers to anonymously report any potential acts of unlawful interference or other violations of freedom of association and collective bargaining rights, and timely investigate any allegations.

Background

The United States Trade Representative and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On July 29, 2025, the ILC received an RRM petition from a group of former and current Alimentos Grole workers affiliated with SITIES. The petition alleged that Alimentos Grole had violated workers’ rights by threatening and dismissing workers to discourage union activity and by forming and promoting a company-aligned internal union. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days. The ILC determined that there was sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms.  

As a result, on August 28, 2025, the United States submitted a request that Mexico review the matter. Mexico agreed to conduct a review and, on October 10, 2025, concluded a denial of the rights had occurred at the facility. Subsequently, the United States and Mexico agreed on a course of remediation. The United States closely monitored compliance with the course of remediation and has concluded the situation to have been remedied.

Read the full course of remediation here.

item.title: Governments and Faith Communities: Supporting the Economic Fundamentals of “The Good Life”
item.description:
Governments and Faith Communities: Supporting the Economic Fundamentals of “The Good Life” pbrouillette Fri, 10/16/2026 - 12:57

As Prepared for Delivery on October 16, 2026

G20 Interfaith Forum

Good morning. Thank you for that generous introduction. 

I am honored and humbled to address this group and its distinguished attendees.  Although I was born and raised in California, my ancestors and many of my extended family have lived in the great Mountain West of the United States, and as a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints I share the faith tradition that was nurtured in the mountains and valleys here in Utah.  But my comments today do not represent the Church, nor do they represent the faith-related policies of the Trump Administration.  Rather, I am here to talk about economic policies that will lift people up across the globe.  

Almost all faith traditions believe that God expects us to work.  Work is not only a moral imperative; it is also a blessing to individuals, families, and communities.  At the same time, heaven is not a counting house where God tallies every nickel and dime and measures our worth by our earthly balance sheets.  Our economic activity – individually and in communities – should reflect deeper meaning.

In addition, world religions teach us that God expects people of faith to help the poor and the needy, and not to stand in judgment of them.

These teachings can sometimes seem to be in tension.  But this tension can be resolved.  Governments and religious communities can, in fact, help people meet the material needs of this life while also contributing to their spiritual well-being.  Today, I want to address two overarching questions:

The first question is really a two-parter: (1) what kind of society are we trying to create, and (2) what are the economic policies that can support that society?

The second question is: what can faith communities do to support economic policies that are the most likely to achieve the type of society that will benefit the broadest portion of humanity?  

So I will first discuss, what kind of society do we want?  

Many of our brightest thinkers have discussed this question, with Aristotle and his successors asking “what is the good life?,” or in the more modern parlance of Joseph Stiglitz, “what is gross domestic product good for?”  

So a lot of ink has been spilled on this topic, but I think average people know the answer.  The Pew Charitable Trust Research Center did a global survey in 2021 asking people across age groups and countries what provides the most meaning in life.  The universal answer was family first, generally followed by either an occupation or material well-being.   Respondents in the United States and United Kingdom ranked “friends” in the number 2 spot.  And you would not be surprised to know that older survey participants rated good health higher than younger participants.  

So this is the kind of society we want: one where people can form a family and relationships and also have meaningful work that allows them to obtain a home and achieve social and economic mobility.  

I would say that an unspoken dynamic here as well is that people want all of these things together, meaning they want to be able to live with or by their family and friends as they achieve their economic goals.  It’s unsatisfying and challenging to have one without the other.

A thriving society like this results in strong community cohesion and a shared sense of purpose.  Communities with robust opportunities for work and production are safer than other communities, and they become high-trust societies with low crime and better health and educational outcomes.   Importantly, these types of societies value families and children.  Policymakers should support economic policies that will promote these outcomes.  

Economic policies of course can lead to negative outcomes.  For example, here in the United States, and in my own line of work, we are attempting to remedy previous international trade policies that had a negative effect on certain populations.  For several decades, U.S. companies took advantage of laissez-faire trade policies to move manufacturing and production from the United States to other countries for a variety of reasons.  

This left many Americans previously employed in factories and plants without jobs in their hometowns.  Recent studies by David Autor and co-authors show that these policies resulted in unemployment and underemployment among those that lost their jobs to offshoring.  Studies by economists from the University of Chicago and University of Wisconsin showed that the North American Free Trade Agreement resulted in negative health outcomes among workers in the United States where that trade agreement changed the fabric of the local economy.   Thus, we have had entire communities where the loss of a factory meant lost income for parents, fewer opportunities for children, and second-order effects of increased drug abuse and premature deaths.  

In the United States, we are trying to change our policies to avoid these outcomes and promote a society that is fulfilling: one where people can develop relationships with family and friends while meeting their economic needs.

To achieve this type of society I believe you also need to ensure national and domestic security, you need good health and education policy, and you need political rights and freedom of religion and expression.  I won’t talk about those today, but I will attempt to answer the question of what kind of economy and economic policies can support a thriving and fulfilling society?  

The global economy and international economic policy should operate to bless society, and not the other way around.

Capitalism, market economics, and the protection of intellectual property have led to enormous welfare gains.  I take the United States as an example: a long-term commitment to free enterprise has lifted entire generations out of poverty.  In 2025, the poverty rate in the United States dropped to 10.2 percent – the lowest since we started tracking these data in 1959.

However, economic policy should not prioritize efficiency and profit-maximizing at all costs.  There are quantifiable (and non-quantifiable) harms from extreme libertarian economic policies.  For example, unregulated concentration of production can limit opportunities for new entrants or harm consumers, workers may suffer from severe power imbalances in the employment relationship, and firms may engage in business practices that disregard economic or national security.  

On the other hand, certain economic policies notionally designed to correct for excesses of capitalism can actually degrade the well-being of individuals, families, and communities.  This may include the seizure of private property, suffocating taxation, and corruption that can arise from government interference in private business.

A responsibility of government is to find the right balance among economic policies.  Even though we live in an imperfect world, governments can promote economic policies that increase the chance for all to live the good life:

Governments must recognize and encourage the worth of individuals and families as producers, and not just as consumers. Governments should enact policies that help people create wealth, as opposed to simply allocating it or consuming it.  Most economic activity fundamentally begins with a person taking something out of the earth and making something of it: crops from the soil, fish from the sea, and minerals from the ground below us.  From these resources, we forge tools and machinery, we process food and drink, and we create chemicals and engineer solutions that prolong life and bring convenience.  In short, we generate wealth that can translate into well-being.

But in many developed countries, a rush towards financialization and speculation has reduced our focus on manufacturing, agriculture, and the associated services.  This trend has turned many of our brightest students to financial wizardry, high-risk derivatives, and unstable Ponzi schemes or multi-level marketing scams.  And as some societies shifted away from production, people also began to feel less like participants in the system and more like victims of it.  

Instead of generating wealth, the United States and other countries have focused on attempting to print wealth and allocate it around the economy, with middlemen taking their share off the top with each new financial instrument.  Obviously, there is a strong need for reliable financial services to help guide capital to its most efficient use, but this must stand on the foundation of the creation of capital in the first place.

In Judaism, the concept of Yishuv ha-olam emphasizes that we are to settle or help establish a sustainable world.  We are to be stewards of the world we have been given, and not only receivers.  In the Book of Genesis, Adam is placed in Eden "to dress it and keep it."  From our earliest days, we were meant to be producers through our labor, not just consumers.  As we read in the Book of Exodus, in the Ten Commandments, Moses received instructions for the children of Israel: “Six days shalt thou labor and do all thy work.”  We tend to focus on this commandment in relation to the Sabbath—a day of rest—but it of course expects that the other days we will work in a productive capacity.
 
In addition to prioritizing domestic production first and consumption second, government should provide for fair trade and commercial opportunities.

Trade or commerce on its own is not necessarily good or bad: it just is.  The more important question is not just whether enterprise is “free,” but whether it is “fair.”

We have all kinds of policies that address unfairness: antitrust laws, employment and labor laws, anti-corruption efforts, and international trade laws.  They all tend to deal with vast imbalances of economic or other power that can endanger fairness and limit opportunity.  By making thoughtful corrections where market forces do not prioritize the type of outcomes our countries need, policymakers can promote societies where individuals and families can thrive.

And so, after all of that, the remaining question is how can faith communities and leaders support economic policies that help us move toward our desired society?

Some religious communities have promoted economic policies that attempt to find the right balance.  In the United States, we have had faith traditions that promote a political economy based on community cohesion and support.  The Transcendentalists of the 19th century sought to live simply and produce only what was needed for consumption.  The United Order of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints sought to have its participants donate all their material possessions and earnings to the Church for an ecclesiastical redistribution.  Your countries may have had religious groups make similar efforts.  These initiatives have not always been successful, largely due to the imperfection of humanity or structural flaws.  

But these traditions do have a few common themes that are instructive; chief among them is that all should contribute to the community economy as producers first and as consumers second.  This is a blessing as individuals become contributing participants in the economy and not victims of it.  

President Dallin H. Oaks of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints recently observed the relationship between family life and making a productive contribution to society.  In October 2025, he warned that “[p]arental influences have … been diluted by the way in which [many people] earn a living.  In times past, one of the great influences that unified families was the experience of struggling together in pursuit of a common goal—such as taming the wilderness or earning a living.  The family was an organized and conducted unit of economic production.  Today, most families are units of economic consumption, which do not require a high degree of family organization and cooperation.”  As faith communities support families, and support families working together, they will support economic policies that have a broader beneficial effect on society.

Faith communities can also create a fulfilling economy by promoting self-reliance.  Contributions to workforce initiatives, training programs, and welfare-to-work programs can answer God’s call to help the needy while also dignifying them as producers and participants in the economy.  Leading people to become self-reliant can succor the immediate needs of those in distress while providing them a long-term pathway to partaking in the good life that we all seek.

Religious communities should also support the rule of law by encouraging their members to be civically active and responsible. This may seem unrelated to economics, but a fair and just legal system helps create trust that the economic system will be fair and equitable.  

Without this bedrock, it can be difficult for members of a society to believe that they will benefit from the economy, and they may worry that the system is “rigged,” as some say.

Finally, it is critical that faith communities discourage harmful economic behavior, both at the institutional and individual levels.

Practices such as financial speculation and highly-leveraged, high-risk economic activities can put entire swathes of an economy in trouble.  Religious communities should also highlight and fight human rights violations that create perverse economic incentives, such as the scourge of forced labor, and they should fight corruption and dishonesty in all its forms.

Religious communities should also combat vice that harms the family economy.  This can include addictive gambling, which can bankrupt individuals and families with the illusion of generating wealth.  Faith communities should also encourage their members to live within their means, taking a lesson from Joseph in Egypt who warned Pharaoh to put up seven years of storage to prepare for the eventual famine.  As people—or countries—turn to credit to support extravagant lifestyles, faith leaders should promote wise stewardship of taxpayer and family funds and preach against envy and greed.

We welcome a gathering like this that can help combine good faith efforts to implement beneficial economic policies with the wisdom and long-term perspective of faith leaders like you.  While business leaders focus on the next quarter, you are looking to eternity.  I ask you to have patience with your political leaders as they try to do what is best for their people.  And I ask you to do your part to help create fulfilling societies where individuals, families, communities, and entire nations can thrive.

Thank you, and I look forward to the rest of the discussion.

item.title: United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Carolina Performance Fabrics
item.description:
United States Seeks Mexico’s Review of Alleged Denial of Workers’ Rights at Carolina Performance Fabrics pbrouillette Tue, 10/13/2026 - 15:03

WASHINGTON — The Office of the United States Trade Representative has invoked the Rapid Response Labor Mechanism (RRM) in the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) to review whether workers at Carolina Performance Fabrics, S.A. de C.V. (Carolina), located in the state of Guanajuato, Mexico, are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The United States has suspended liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from the Carolina facility, which manufactures specialized, high-performance textiles for the automotive industry.

Background

The United States Trade Representative (Trade Representative) and the Secretary of Labor co-chair the Interagency Labor Committee for Monitoring and Enforcement (ILC). On September 10, 2026, the ILC received an RRM petition from a Mexican union affiliated with the Confederación Central Nacional (COCENA). The petition alleges that Carolina has violated workers’ rights by interfering in union activity and retaliating against workers because of their attempts to organize for COCENA, including through harassment, threats, and unlawful dismissals. The ILC reviews RRM petitions that it receives, and the accompanying information, within 30 days.

After conducting this review, the ILC determined that there is sufficient, credible evidence of a denial of rights enabling the good faith invocation of enforcement mechanisms under the USMCA. As a result, the Trade Representative has submitted a request to Mexico under Annex 31-A of the USMCA that Mexico review whether workers at Carolina are being denied the right to freedom of association and collective bargaining. The Trade Representative has also directed the Secretary of the Treasury to suspend liquidation of unliquidated entries of goods from Carolina.

Mexico has 10 days to agree to conduct a review and, if it agrees, 45 days from today to complete the review.

A copy of the request for review can be found here.

A copy of the letter to the Secretary of the Treasury can be found here.

Information about previous requests can be found here.
